Venmo could face disruption from Elon Musk’s X Money service. Unveiled last month, X Money is an X-based fund transfer service. If successfully implemented, it could compete with Venmo for peer-to-peer transfers.

PayPal (PYPL) shares have gained 30.2% over the past six months, compared with 1.8% for the S&P 500. Investors who bought into management’s turnaround are banking on fast growth from Venmo, Pay Later and other financial services, while relying on the PayPal checkout button to at least keep its pace. The newer businesses command the spotlight, but the checkout button is where the risk sits. So how is the checkout button holding up?

During the October 27, 2026 call, management said payment volume through the checkout button has grown between 1% and 2% for four quarters. The volume is neither shrinking nor accelerating. Management also said the end of an EU tax exemption known as de minimis affected some merchants, creating about 70 basis points of headwind to checkout volume growth.

There are brighter spots. Management said U.S. checkout volume improved for the third quarter in a row, and Germany stabilized. Still, management expects the same 1%-2% growth through the fourth quarter because it assumes the headwinds in Europe continue.

Management’s own plan does not ask much of the button. It said it expects checkout volume to improve, though its growth plan does not require a full return to historical growth rates. So far, the button has held its pace.
Not yet. Transaction margin dollars grew about 2% in fiscal Q3 2026. Management calls growth in this profit measure its North Star, aiming for mid-single-digit growth over time.

The faster businesses are real. Management said financial services already make up more than 20% of transaction margin dollars and are growing at double digits. Venmo’s payment volume has also grown at double digits for eight quarters in a row.

PayPal's Venmo Grows in Q3: Can Rising Monetization Fuel Earnings?
sum: PayPal Holdings, Inc. PYPL continued to witness strong momentum in its Venmo business during the third quarter of 2026, supported by higher payment volumes, increased engagement and growing adoption of monetized services. Venmo's total payment volume (TPV) rose 14% year over year to $96.8 billion from $85.2 billion, marking its eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth.

Venmo accounted for 20% of PayPal's total payment volume during the quarter, up from 19% a year earlier. The platform's growth reflects increasing adoption of its debit card and Pay with Venmo offerings. Pay with Venmo TPV rose 43% year over year, highlighting growing consumer demand for using the service beyond peer-to-peer payments.

Venmo's debit card business also gained momentum, with monthly active accounts rising more than 55% year over year to 6.7 million. The platform added a record 1.6 million first-time debit card users during the third quarter. Moreover, debit card payment volume increased more than 60%, reflecting stronger spending activity and deeper customer engagement.

Monetization remains a key growth opportunity. Venmo's average revenue per active account (ARPA) increased at a double-digit rate, supported by rising adoption of financial services. Notably, debit card users generate five to six times higher ARPA than peer-to-peer-only users. With just 23% of Venmo customers using financial services, further adoption could support higher revenues and transaction margins.

For PayPal, Venmo's expansion is strengthening overall profitability. Transaction margin dollars increased 2% year over year to $3.95 billion, while non-GAAP earnings rose 8% to $1.45 per share. Management raised its full-year 2026 non-GAAP EPS guidance to approximately $5.60 from $5.38, reflecting improving earnings expectations.

Block, Inc.’s XYZ Cash App competes with PayPal’s Venmo in peer-to-peer payments while offering debit spending, merchant payments and financial services. Its Neighborhoods initiative connects Cash App users with Square merchants, supporting engagement and payment adoption. In third-quarter 2026, Cash App gross profit increased 27% year over year to $2.07 billion.

Is PayPal Stock Ready For A Year Of Higher Spending?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

On October 27, 2026, PayPal (PYPL) raised its 2026 forecast for adjusted earnings per share to $5.60 from $5.38. During the company’s earnings call that day, management said PayPal plans to invest further in 2027. Executives intend to invest in operating expenses and spend transaction margin dollars, which are the profit PayPal keeps after covering the costs of each payment. For a shareholder, these investments compete with the profit that funds PayPal’s buybacks. So how much of PayPal’s profit could a costlier 2027 take?

If PayPal reinvested all of the cost savings it expects by the end of 2026, that money would equal at least 11% of the $6.35 billion in operating income it earned in the four quarters to September 30, 2026. Management expects those cost cuts to reach an annual run rate of more than $700 million by the end of 2026, and said it intends to reinvest a significant portion of that money. That 11% assumes PayPal reinvests all of the savings, so the share it actually puts back is likely smaller. It excludes the transaction margin dollars management also plans to invest in 2027.

PayPal’s incentive spending is already visible in its revenue. The company’s revenue grew 2.0% in fiscal Q3 2026, compared with 7.3% in the same quarter a year earlier. Management said higher contra revenue investments, which are incentives booked as a cut to revenue, partially held that growth back, alongside the EU’s removal of a tax exemption on low-value imports.

Management also said it underwrites its branded checkout investments to about a two- to three-year horizon, noting that the savings and the new spending will not align quarter by quarter. PayPal plans to direct this money into areas such as financial services and specialized sales teams.

PayPal generated $6.3 billion of free cash flow in the four quarters to September 30, 2026, and spent $6.05 billion of it repurchasing its own shares. With almost all of that cash funding buybacks, the pace of those repurchases, rather than the debt, looks like what a costlier year would affect first.
PayPal’s net debt is small relative to that cash flow.

Peter Thiel Was an Early Outside Investor in Facebook and Co-Founded Both PayPal and Palantir Before Building a Hedge Fund Now Concentrated in Power and Energy Stocks. Here's What That Track Record Says About Following His Contrarian Bets.
sum: Wall Street is always looking for the next guru. But market history is filled with investors who scored big once, or even a few times, and then faded from history because they didn't keep hitting home runs. That's important to keep in mind as you consider the big shift toward electric stocks in Peter Thiel's portfolio.

Peter Thiel is a famous investor thanks to his successful investments in the technology sector, including Facebook (now called Meta (META +2.36%)). He also helped found PayPal (PYPL -0.97%) and Palantir (PLTR -1.65%). There's a good reason to listen to Thiel when it comes to investing, particularly in the technology sector.

However, you don't want to forget that even good investors make mistakes. Warren Buffett, the longtime CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.22%)(BRKB +0.17%) was famous for pointing out his missteps even though his investment approach had been incredibly successful over the long term. Simply put, just because an investor is famous, it doesn't mean you should blindly follow them. They are human, just like you.

What Peter Thiel's shift into energy tells you is that you may want to consider following him... after you do your own homework. As your parents probably asked when you were a kid, "If your friend jumped off a cliff, would you jump too?" When it comes to investing, too many people follow without thinking. You don't want to be one of them.

In this situation, Peter Thiel might be on to something. Electricity demand grew 10% between 2005 and 2025, but is expected to climb 60% between 2025 and 2045. That's a step change in demand driven by new technologies like artificial intelligence and electric vehicles. Thiel clearly knows a thing or two about technology and how the industry operates, so a deep dive into electric stocks is probably a good idea.

On that front, Thiel's purchases included independent power producers American Electric Power (AEP -0.36%) and Vistra (VST +3.70%). It also included utility CMS Energy (CMS -1.07%) and nuclear power start-up X-Energy (XE +5.88%). There's a lot going on in that mix, and it might be hard for investors with jobs and lives outside the stock market to dig into and understand all the companies Thiel has chosen to own.

PayPal Shares Tumble 12.7% as Stripe-Advent Group Abandons $53 Billion Bid
sum: PayPal Holdings Inc. (PYPL) shares fell 12.71% on Thursday after Bloomberg News reported that a consortium of Stripe and private equity firm Advent International had walked away from a takeover bid that valued the digital payments pioneer at more than $53 billion.

The stock closed at $53.66, down from $61.47 the previous day. In pre-market trading, the decline briefly reached 16%, underscoring how much investor enthusiasm had been tied to the prospect of a deal. Since reports of the acquisition talks first surfaced in mid-July, PayPal shares had climbed nearly 30%.

Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, said late Wednesday that the buyout group was no longer pursuing the company. The situation remains fluid, according to the same report, and the consortium could still return with a revised offer at a later date. Advent, Stripe, and PayPal all declined to comment.

The proposed transaction, first reported in July, would have valued PayPal at $60.50 per share, or roughly $53 billion. It was backed by about $50 billion in committed bank financing and would have given Stripe and Advent equal ownership stakes. A combined entity would have processed approximately $3.7 trillion in annual payment volume by merging Stripe's merchant network with PayPal's consumer ecosystem.

Before the abandonment was reported, the Wall Street Journal said PayPal had viewed the initial offer as insufficient and that the two sides were negotiating over price. Thursday's closing price of $53.66 sits well below the $60.50 per share that had been on the table.

PayPal has struggled in recent years with slowing growth and intensifying competition from Apple Pay and Google Pay. In response, the San Jose-based company has reshuffled its leadership, cut jobs, and trimmed costs in an effort to restore profitability. The stock remains a shadow of its pandemic-era peak, when the company's market capitalization reached about $356 billion in 2021.

The failed pursuit comes just days after Stripe agreed to pay $8 billion for AI model marketplace OpenRouter. A source told Axios that the OpenRouter and PayPal deals were operating on independent tracks and that the end of the PayPal talks was unrelated to that acquisition.

PYPL’s Historical Floor Is Back, But Is The Business The Same?
sum: PayPal’s stock has returned to a price zone that has historically launched powerful rallies, after trading well below it as recently as last month

PayPal (PYPL) moves money, powering online checkouts and peer-to-peer payments through its app and services like Venmo. Today, its stock sits at about $58.54 a share, squarely inside a price zone between $55.61 and $61.47 that has served as a floor for the company’s shares 6 separate times.

History at this level has been explosive. The critical question for investors watching the stock climb back into this familiar ground is a simple one: will this level hold as support, or does it stall out again here?

A defended level on a chart is a memory of where demand overwhelmed supply. For PayPal, the memory here is potent. Buyers have successfully defended this price zone on 6 prior occasions, sparking rallies that produced an average peak gain of 92%.

These ranged from modest to explosive, from single-digit bounces to a 406% surge, with a typical gain in the mid-20s%. More recently, a defense on 7/1/2024 led to a 59% gain. The consistency of these past episodes is what draws the eye now; this is a historically defended support level where buyers have previously shown conviction.

A floor holds or breaks based on the health of the business standing on it. While PayPal’s growth engines like Venmo and Braintree are delivering, with total payment volume growing in the mid-teens, the company is fundamentally different than it was during prior tests of this level. The core branded checkout business, once its unstoppable force, has seen its growth stabilize at just 2% for a second consecutive quarter.

This slowdown is the reason the stock fell into this zone in the first place, and it forms the honest catch for anyone relying on history to repeat. Management has embarked on a multiyear transformation to diversify into financial services, funded by at least $1.5 billion in cost savings. Yet this plan faces a wall of doubt, with one analyst on the company’s latest call noting that “strategies and investments haven’t necessarily materialized.” This turnaround effort is, in essence, a bet against Wall Street skepticism, a topic explored in a recent analysis of the company’s strategy.

If PayPal continues expanding the adoption of Pay with Venmo, the Venmo Debit Card and merchant checkout, Venmo could become a significantly larger revenue driver over time.
